content.title: How to Start Practicing Islam in the Family?
content.subtitle: Avoiding Satan's Traps & A Sunnah Guide to Family Deen
content.body:
Understanding the Deen correctly is a great blessing from Allah. When the light of faith enters one’s life after years of heedlessness, and one begins praying Tahajjud and performing good deeds, the heart finds peace. Yet Satan begins attacking from two directions:

  • Showing Off (Riya): Satan whispers that hidden acts of worship—Tahajjud, charity, or tears during dua—should somehow be revealed to one’s spouse, friends, or on Facebook. He continually tempts the heart to publicize these deeds.

  • Pride and Contempt: After beginning to practice Islam, a person may unknowingly become arrogant and look down on others, thinking, “I worship so much, while they keep sleeping! What kind of believer are they?”

These two attitudes can seriously undermine the good deeds of Muslim brothers and sisters.

A Gradual, Sunnah-Based Approach to Practicing Islam as a Family

1. Avoid Forcing Change Overnight; Be Consistent

After listening to an Islamic lecture or attending a gathering of knowledge, many people feel a sudden surge of God-consciousness and spiritual enthusiasm. They may want to bring their entire family into an active Islamic lifestyle immediately. But imposing changes in haste can create misunderstandings and distance instead of peace at home.

Remember, I may have understood the Deen after 20 or 40 years of my life. My children were not raised in that environment from the beginning, so they cannot be transformed overnight. Allah prohibited alcohol in the Qur’an in three stages—through indication, warning, and final prohibition. Similarly, guiding a family toward Islam requires love, patience, and gradual progress over weeks, months, or years—not impulsive demands.

2. First Step: Improve Your Own Deeds and Character

To make your family more practicing, begin by practicing Islam yourself and visibly improving your character and behavior.

  • Establish your prayers regularly.

  • Ensure you are not treating your spouse unjustly.

  • Make your temperament, thoughts, and dealings fair and just.

  • Only after improving your own character should you invite your family toward the Deen.

3. Tahajjud and Your Spouse’s Right to Sleep

Encouraging each other to pray Tahajjud and gently waking a spouse by sprinkling water is undoubtedly a beautiful Sunnah practice. Its true beauty, however, lies in gentleness and mutual understanding. Forcing an exhausted spouse to wake up after a hard day does not reflect the balanced teachings of the Sunnah. An invitation to worship should never become a source of emotional pressure or hardship.

The Prophet ﷺ would rise so quietly for Tahajjud that he would not disturb Aisha (RA), who was sleeping beside him. She would not even realize he had begun praying until his feet touched her in the darkness during prostration.

A Practical Tip: Instead of suddenly demanding Tahajjud, plan ahead one or two nights a week: “Whoever wakes up first will gently wake the other.” This creates mental preparation and helps build the habit with love.

4. Balance Household Responsibilities and Care for Each Other

  • If a wife is exhausted and asleep after a full day of household work, her husband should respect her need for rest.

  • Likewise, a husband who works all day at a shop, job, or office needs proper sleep. Otherwise, his performance may suffer, potentially causing problems or demotion at work. His wife should also be mindful of his rest.

Practicing Islam requires balance, not haste. Faith cannot be imposed on someone overnight. Through good character, wisdom, and gradual, loving encouragement, a family can be guided toward the light of Islam.

These points are taken from a lecture by Ustadh Atik Ullah (Hafizahullah). May Allah grant the Shaykh a blessed life and enable us to act upon his guidance. Ameen.
